title: Gemstone Dowsing
statementMd:
Rockhounding is the hobby of searching for valuable rocks and gemstones in the natural environment. As a national-level rockhound yourself, you're determined to find the most valuable gem possible!

You've found an area of land whose cross section can be modeled by a 2D Euclidean plane with the ground at the line $y = 0$. Everything below this line is solid stone, and everything above is air. Buried within the stone are $N$ rare gemstones, each at a (potentially non-unique) $(x, y)$ location with $y \lt 0$.

Some of these gemstones have already been traced by other rockhounds, who have claimed their discovery by publishing their locations (while leaving the stones themselves in place). That still leaves some gemstones for you to find!

To actually find gemstones, you plan to use an oscilloscope to detect waveforms emitted by each gem. Each gem has a unique frequency that can be measured from a distance; however, this specific oscilloscope has a quirk in that each time it is used, it only records the frequency emitted by the **closest gem**, using Euclidean distance. In the case of a tie, it arbitrarily picks a frequency emitted by one of the closest gems.

![image](https://espresso.codeforces.com/740c8db19759d9c0765c53fd44c26d0c3bc99f32.png)An illustration of Sample Input 1. Gem icons underground represent previously discovered gemstones, and points on the surface indicate your oscilloscope readings.

You've just used the oscilloscope $N$ times at various **unique** locations $(x_j, 0)$ on the surface of the Earth. You recorded these locations along with the frequency $f_j$ detected by the oscilloscope at that location. Interestingly enough, you've noticed that the frequency of **every gemstone appears exactly once** in your records.

Of the gems that haven't yet been discovered by other rockhounds, you'd like to find the most valuable one. And of course, the deeper the gem, the more valuable!

A plausible configuration of the gemstones is a placement of each undiscovered gemstone on the 2D Euclidean plane that satisfies the following conditions:

- every gemstone is underground ($y \lt 0$);
- for every oscilloscope reading of frequency $f_j$ at location $(x_j,0)$, no gemstone is closer to $(x_j,0)$ in Euclidean distance than the gemstone with frequency $f_j$.

You wish to calculate, for each yet-undiscovered gemstone, the deepest possible (most negative) $y$-coordinate of that gem among all plausible configurations of gemstones.

## Input

The first line contains two space-separated integers $N$ $(2 \le N \le 10^5)$ and $K$ $(1 \le K \le N - 1)$: the number of buried gemstones (and oscilloscope readings) and number of those gemstones that have already been discovered by other rockhounds, respectively.

Each of the next $K$ lines contains three space-separated integers $x_i$ $(|x_i| \le 10^6)$, $y_i$ $(-10^6 \le y_i \lt 0)$, and $f_i$ $(1 \le f_i \le N)$, describing the location and frequency of a gemstone that has already been discovered. It is possible that two or more gemstones occupy the same location. It is guaranteed that the $f_i$ values are unique.

Finally, each of the last $N$ lines contains two space-separated integers $x_j$ $(|x_j| \le 10^6)$ and $f_j$ $(1 \le f_j \le N)$, describing an oscilloscope reading. It is guaranteed that the $x_j$ values are unique, that they are listed in increasing order, and that every gemstone (discovered and undiscovered) has exactly one oscilloscope reading. It is also guaranteed that there is at least one plausible configuration of gemstones.

## Output

For each of the $N-K$ undiscovered gemstones, print a line with an integer and a negative real number: the frequency $f_\ell$ of the gemstone and the deepest (most negative) possible $y$-coordinate $y_\ell$ of that gemstone among all plausible configurations of the gemstones. It can be proved that this deepest possible $y$-coordinate exists for every undiscovered gemstone and is negative and finite.

You may print these lines in any order. Your answer will be accepted if each depth value you assign to an undiscovered gemstone differs from the judge solution by relative or absolute error at most $10^{-5}$.
statementZhMd:
在自然环境中寻找有价值的岩石和宝石是一种业余爱好。作为一名国家级的宝石搜寻爱好者，你决心找到价值最高的宝石！

你发现了一片土地，其横截面可以用二维欧几里得平面建模，地面位于直线 $y = 0$ 上。这条直线下方全是坚硬的岩石，上方则是空气。岩石中埋藏着 $N$ 颗稀有宝石，每颗宝石都位于某个 $y \lt 0$ 的位置 $(x, y)$，不同宝石的位置可能相同。

其中一些宝石已经被其他宝石搜寻者探明，他们通过公布宝石的位置来宣告自己的发现（但仍将宝石留在原处）。不过，仍有一些宝石等待你去发现！

为了找到宝石，你打算使用示波器来检测每颗宝石发出的波形。每颗宝石都有一个独特的频率，可以从远处测量；然而，这台示波器有一个特殊之处：每次使用时，它只会记录按欧几里得距离计算的**最近的宝石**所发出的频率。如果有多颗宝石并列最近，它会任意选择其中一颗宝石发出的频率。

![image](https://espresso.codeforces.com/740c8db19759d9c0765c53fd44c26d0c3bc99f32.png)样例输入 1 的示意图。地下的宝石图标表示此前已被发现的宝石，地表上的点表示你使用示波器进行测量的位置。

你刚刚在地表上 $N$ 个**互不相同**的位置 $(x_j, 0)$ 使用了示波器。你记录了这些位置，以及示波器在各位置检测到的频率 $f_j$。有趣的是，你发现**每颗宝石的频率都恰好在记录中出现一次**。

对于那些尚未被其他宝石搜寻者发现的宝石，你想找到其中价值最高的一颗。当然，宝石埋得越深，就越有价值！

一种合理的宝石布局，是指在二维欧几里得平面上为每颗尚未被发现的宝石安排位置，并满足以下条件：

- 每颗宝石都位于地下（$y \lt 0$）；
- 对于在位置 $(x_j,0)$ 测得频率 $f_j$ 的每条示波器记录，任何宝石到 $(x_j,0)$ 的欧几里得距离都不小于频率为 $f_j$ 的宝石到该位置的距离。

对于每颗尚未被发现的宝石，你希望计算：在所有合理的宝石布局中，该宝石所能达到的最深位置的 $y$ 坐标（即最小的 $y$ 坐标）。

## 输入格式

第一行包含两个以空格分隔的整数 $N$ $(2 \le N \le 10^5)$ 和 $K$ $(1 \le K \le N - 1)$，分别表示埋藏的宝石数量（也是示波器的测量次数），以及其中已被其他宝石搜寻者发现的宝石数量。

接下来的 $K$ 行，每行包含三个以空格分隔的整数 $x_i$ $(|x_i| \le 10^6)$、$y_i$ $(-10^6 \le y_i \lt 0)$ 和 $f_i$ $(1 \le f_i \le N)$，描述一颗已被发现的宝石的位置和频率。两颗或更多宝石可能位于同一位置。保证所有 $f_i$ 的值互不相同。

最后的 $N$ 行，每行包含两个以空格分隔的整数 $x_j$ $(|x_j| \le 10^6)$ 和 $f_j$ $(1 \le f_j \le N)$，描述一条示波器测量记录。保证所有 $x_j$ 的值互不相同，且按递增顺序给出；每颗宝石（包括已被发现和尚未被发现的宝石）都恰好对应一条示波器测量记录。还保证至少存在一种合理的宝石布局。

## 输出格式

对于 $N-K$ 颗尚未被发现的宝石中的每一颗，输出一行，包含一个整数和一个负实数：该宝石的频率 $f_\ell$，以及在所有合理的宝石布局中，该宝石所能达到的最深位置的 $y$ 坐标 $y_\ell$（即最小的 $y$ 坐标）。可以证明，对于每颗尚未被发现的宝石，这个最深位置的 $y$ 坐标都存在，且为有限的负数。

你可以按任意顺序输出这些行。如果你为每颗尚未被发现的宝石给出的深度值与标准答案的相对误差或绝对误差不超过 $10^{-5}$，则你的答案将被接受。
